utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was told to wait in the witness room for courtroom 3 so I think that's where the usher has gone to get him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour may I raise a matter before he comes in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hope it's only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's only one. I notice from the list of documents that the Prosecutor proposes to use with regard to this witness, that they mention several of the intercepts. These documents have not been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Disclosed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They have been disclosed but they have not been admitted as exhibits and I have rather strong objection to those intercepts because I believe they were done contrary to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, illegally done, and therefore should not be admitted before Your Honours and therefore I would object to their being used with this witness on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman has in the course of conversations mentioned this but we've had absolutely no warning that there is an objection or that there is any conflict over the legality of these because the intercept witnesses are actually going to be starting tomorrow, and we've had no notice of this. No legal motion has been filed on this. So that's the situation. I suggest Mr. Ackerman files this fairly quickly or raises it fairly quickly because these witnesses are here to testify from tomorrow onwards, and we can't waste time on legal submissions that they shouldn't be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I'm making it very clear at this point that telling us, "Because I believe they were done contrary to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, illegally done," is not enough in itself. It's so vague, unless you come up with something really substantial, indicating where precisely the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been violated, by whom, and whether that should necessarily bring us to the conclusion not to admit these intercepts just the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'd ask if there is going to be -- it be done in writing, what we don't want to do is waste valuable court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I agree with you, Ms. Korner. I agree with you. So I am going to admit these intercepts until I have enough, sufficient reasons forthcoming from you to substantiate what you are alleging, telling me, "I believe that they were obtained in an illegal manner" alone without substantiating that statement is not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I understand that. It was only late last night that I became aware there was an intent on the Prosecutor's part to use them with this particular witness. I thought they were going to be dealt with with the witnesses that are coming tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was in the process of preparing exactly what you're suggesting and that is an objection. It's always been my view that the time to object to exhibits is when the Prosecutor makes it clear they are going to offer them and that seems to be clear with regard to the coming witnesses and I'm prepared to make a more detailed objection at that time but I didn't bring the documents with me this morning. But I'll have something in writing in your hands before the day is out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, but in the meantime I'm going to admit them with the caveat that I mentioned. You can rest assured, Mr. Ackerman, that if there is an illegality, we go into it, but it doesn't necessarily mean that the illegality means expunging the documents or not having them admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm also aware of that, Your Honour. This matter was heavily dealt with in an earlier case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly it has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So where is Mr. Treanor? I must also admit that I haven't seen any of these documents as yet, the intercepts. I haven't even come across them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And saying welcome to this Tribunal is a little bit of a misnomer. You are about to give testimony in the case which has been instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin. You are here as an expert witness for the Prosecution. I suppose that you are not new to the proceedings before this Tribunal. For the time being, what is required from you is to make the solemn declaration provided for in the rules and namely to speak the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth in the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, please take a chair. I don't know if you have been informed but you will not be cross-examined at this point. You will be cross-examined in a couple of months' time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've understood that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I understand, will be examining you in chief. Thank you. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sir could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Joseph Treanor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: 14 February, 1949.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can a break please be made between question and answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland, Mr. Treanor --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You both speak English and if you don't allow a short interval of time between question and answer, the interpreters will find it very difficult to catch up with you. So please try to help the interpreters as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did you -- do you have a Bachelor of Arts degree in modern languages from the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, U.S.A. and you gained that in 1968?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in Worcester, Massachusetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also have a masters degree in Russian and East European studies from Yale University in New Haven in the United States and you gained that in 1970?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also have a doctorate of philosophy from the University College of London, University of London, United Kingdom, you gained that in 1999, after completing a course of study at the school of Slavonic and East European studies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to deal briefly with your relevant work experience. From 1977 until 1980, you worked as an intelligence analyst in the federal research division of the U.S. Library of Congress?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your work involved analysis of Yugoslav military and related affairs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From late 1980 until 1994 you worked as a historian and later senior historian in the office of special investigations of the United States Department of Justice?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This office had the mandate to investigate and litigate cases of persons living in or attempting to gain entry to the United States and alleged to have participated in Nazi persecution during the years 1933 to 1945?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it did and it still does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And much of the work related to the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From July, 1994, or in July, 1994, you commenced working for the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal as a research officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since February, 1998 you have been leader of the leadership research team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As leader of the LRT, is it common practice for you to supervise the production of reports for investigations and trial teams?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that you have more experience than others in the section with respect to war crimes-related matters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I've been working in that area as was mentioned earlier, since 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does anyone in the section have higher academic qualifications than yourself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I don't believe so. There are several others that have Ph.D's as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you've been working in the area since 1980, war crimes area. How many years have you spent researching and analysing documentary collections?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, I first started doing documentary research in my student days, probably going back at least to 1970. On a professional basis I became involved in doing documentary research when I joined the U.S. Department of Justice in 1980. In the course of my employment there of over 13 years, I did research in any number of archives in several countries, including of course the United States, but also the United Kingdom, Germany, former Yugoslavia, the former Soviet Union and Israel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many years have you spent researching and analysing Bosnian Serb or Serb documentation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I've been involved with that documentation since very shortly after my arrival at the Tribunal, since the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So almost nine years?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Almost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed documentary collections with respect to other ethnicities from the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there other people within the LRT who specialise in those matters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, we have people specializing in doing research and analysis in regard to each of the parties to the various conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You prepared a report entitled, "The Bosnian Serb leadership, 1990 to 1992. Addendum. Governing structures in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, 1991, 1992." I would ask that that be admitted into evidence, Your Honours, and if it could be given Exhibit number P2351?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No objection other than with regard to the proposition that there -- I believe there are documents referred to in the footnotes of those reports that are not exhibits in this case, and to the extent that they are being presented to the Trial Chamber in any form, they need to be properly marked and exhibited, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Point taken, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in order to put the addendum report into context, you had prepared an earlier report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The earlier report was prepared in connection with another case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which case was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The -- as it was at that time the Krajisnik Plavsic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that report deals with the structures and how they functioned and the main decision-making process, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it deals with the main political structures that the Bosnian Serbs created in the period 1990 to 1992, including the Serbian Democratic Party and then the governmental structures proper that were created during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to prepare the addendum report? Could you briefly explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution trial team in this case asked me, I believe at the end of 2000, the year 2001, if my unit could prepare a similar report in regard to the governing structures in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which of course we were more than glad to do. By the time that report was fairly well along, the other report had already been submitted in the Krajisnik Plavsic case so there was a bit of overlap and redundancy between the two reports at which point it was decided to make the second report, that is the ARK report, an addendum to the first report and simply put in that report the portions that were different from what was in the main report, covering in particular the governing structures that the -- the main governmental structures of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the ARK region per se.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In writing this report, you were assisted by other members of the LRT?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: In writing both reports, yes, the main report, if we can call it that, and the addendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in writing the addendum report, you were also assisted by another member of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Aguirre, the strategic analyst, assisted in writing section 6 of the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was the only person who was outside my team who worked on that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Ms. Sutherland, according to the submission of Ms. Korner, of the 6th of June, Mr. Aguirre, Xavier Aguirre, did not assist in writing section 6 but he actually wrote section 5. Now, what I have here, Prosecution wishes to point out to the Trial Chamber and the Defence that the report has been written by expert witness, Mr. Treanor, with the assistance of members of his leadership research team, with the exception of section 5 of the report entitled "Municipal implementation of ARK Crisis Staff directives" which has been written by Mr. Xavier Aguirre, a strategic analyst, employed by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I misspoke when I said section 6. I meant section 5. And I take your point that he wrote that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to correct the record. I mean, it's not that important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is right, Mr. Treanor, that in the addendum report you refer back to the -- you refer the reader to the main report for certain sections?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At certain points in the addendum there would be an obvious gap if we did not treat certain subjects which were treated in the main report, so at those points we refer back to the main report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of those sections was dealing with the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is dealt with in the main report. I don't think there is an explicit reference to that section in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And that's where you refer the reader back to the main report. Could you briefly tell the Court how the SDS functioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the SDS was founded in July, 1990, at an assembly at which the party adopted a programme and statutes. The statutes of the party set up a structure which was slightly modified the following year at the second assembly of the party in July, 1991, and they adopted a modified statute. I think we have a copy of the statute available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be provided with the document? It's a new exhibit. Could that be marked P2352?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We marked 2351, the expert's report that you referred him to. Then there was the other report which was the one he had prepared for the Krajisnik Plavsic. Is that going to be tendered as well? Because if it is I suppose that should be the 2352 and not this one. I think it's important that both are tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In order to comprehend the parts in the addendum you need to refer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also because the second one was submitted so that to enable us to understand the first. So I don't see how we can live with one and not with the other. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But I would just like to make clear that there are a number of documents contained in the main report that have not been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because they are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will come to that at the right moment. So that will be 2352, I take it, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The main report and the draft statute of the SDS dated July, 1991 can be P2353.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why draft statute? Is it a draft?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Draft translation of the statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No it's a draft statute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, is it? Yeah P2353, all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor you may continue.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Certainly. First of all to address the issue of the draft statute that is the nature of this document I'd like to make a general observation in regard to the nature of the report which is that it is closely based on documentation on original documents and of course it can only be based on documents that are available to us. Not every document that may have been created that would be of interest to us in connection with the report is in fact available to us. In many of the documents contain various editorial and other imperfections. The document before us now, the statute of the Serbian Democratic Party of 1991 is marked as a proposal. It does however carry the date at the end of the document of 12 July, 1991, which is the date of the second assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party. One of the documents that we do have available to us is the stenographic record of that assembly from which it is apparent that they did adopt the new statute without much discussion. However, we do not have -- we do not happen to have a copy of a document which says statute adopted on this date with a signature. All we have is this proposal, which is presumably what was sent to the delegates to the assembly for their consideration during the meeting. As I say, the stenographic records of the session make it clear that the statute was in fact adopted. So we have used this document as the basis for our analysis of the statutes of the Serbian Democratic Party. In the main report we in fact refer to both of them, the 1990 statute which bears no such notation of being a draft and this one, in order to economise, it seemed appropriate just to use this one. This was the statute that was in force after 1991, after July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take us to the articles in the statute that you deem to be important?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Certainly. I would first of all call attention to Article 1 in the statute, which defines the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a political organisation of the Serbian people and of other ethnic groups that accept the programme and statute of the party. I would also call attention to Article 10 of the Statute which sets out the goals of the party, and it states that the goal of the SDS is to work on the realisation of the interests of the Serbian people, the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and goes on to say, for instance, the interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina are primarily manifested in the struggle for: A, a federation of the federal state of Yugoslavia and a Bosnia-Herzegovina with equal rights within Yugoslavia and the equal rights of all ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the federal state of Yugoslavia. It goes on to speak of its desire for a unified Yugoslav national army, respect for human rights, the rule of law, and close cooperation with the Serbian Orthodox Church. Next I would like to call attention to Article 13 which sets out the rights and duties of members of the Serbian Democratic Party, one of which is to respect and implement the programme and statute of the Serbian Democratic Party. The further articles I'd like to call attention to deal with the internal organisation of the party which I believe was the original question. We could move to Article 19, which states that the organisational forms of the Serbian Democratic Party shall be an assembly and boards in local municipal city and republican organisations. Those are basically the levels of government that existed in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the party is organised -- the party structure is organised to correspond to the structure of governmental bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would next call attention to Article 29, which sets out the internal organs of the party. It says that the SDS organs are as follows: An assembly of the SDS; the president of the SDS; a main board; an executive board; and then also a supervisory board; a statutes council and various councils of the SDS. Those bodies in their composition and duties are described further on in the statute. We could move, for instance, to Article 30, which deals with the assembly of the SDS. This is the body that met as I mentioned in July, 1990 and then again in July, 1991. This Article defines the assembly of the SDS as the highest organ of the SDS and it goes on to specify its composition from representatives of the municipal and other lower assemblies of the SDS. It says it should convene once a year and goes on with some other duties of the assembly in Article 30. And in Article 31 specifies some particular duties of the assembly such as adopting and amending the programme and statute of the party, adopting rules of procedure, electing and dismissing the president of the party, electing and dismissing the main board of the party and similarly for the supervisory board, the statutes council and goes on to specify some other duties of the assembly. Further articles address the other organs of the party, namely Article 32 if we could move to that one, which discusses the president of the SDS. It says that the president of the SDS is by virtue of his position also the president of the main board, specifies that he or she will have a mandate of four years. Article 33 goes on to specify some particular rights and duties of the president of the party which is to represent the party, to ensure the implementation of the programme of the party, to convene the assemblies, to convene the sessions of the main board, to coordinate the activities of organs and bodies of the party, to take political and other decisions on behalf of the party, unless they were within the competence of other organs and bodies of the party, and goes on. Ending with the statement that in extraordinary situations the president could take over extraordinary powers that were within the competence of the assembly and the main board. Now, the main board is described in beginning in Article 35, where the main board is defined as the highest organ of the party between sessions of the assembly. Remember those only met once a year. Article 36 specifies the composition of the main board, which in 1991 was changed to 45 members from I believe the original 52 members. And then Article 37 is one similar to the previous articles for the other bodies which specifies some of the particular duties of the main board such as electing the presidents and two-thirds of the members of the executive board, preparing documents and decisions to be adopted by the assembly of the party, to decide on the territorial organisation of the party, to implement decisions of the assembly, to adopt an election programme of the party, and on and on, ending with providing guidance and adopt decisions for the activities of the lower party levels, that is the municipal, city and local boards of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I've been asked to ask you to slow down a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I believe we can turn to the executive board of the party, which is treated beginning with Article 38 and I think we will call it quits here, this being the last important organ of the party. For present purposes I believe Article 38 defines the executive board as the executive organ of the main board. Article 39 specifies its membership consisting of 15 members some of whom will be elected by the main board and some appointed on the basis of nomination by the president of the party. The -- Article 40 specifies that the members of the main board would be responsible to the main board for their work, and then we have Article 41 which again lists a series of particular rights and duties of the main board such as preparing materials for the needs of -- I'm sorry, the rights and duties of the executive board such as preparing materials for the needs of the main board, adopting its own rules of procedure, to ensure the implementation of decisions of the main board, control over SDS property, and on, ending with to conduct other business entrusted to it by the presidents and the main board. So those are the main organs of the Serbian Democratic Party as set out in its statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of regional boards of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The original 1990 statute made provisions for regions within the party and regional boards were apparently formed and apparently continued to exist even after July, 1991, as coordinating bodies among the municipal organisations, in particular regions, they did not have the same authority, however, that the municipal organisations of the party had, which are defined in the statute. They played merely a coordinating role and did not have the same status within the hierarchy of the party as the other levels I described, the local, municipal and republic level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS participated in the November 1990 elections, did they not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I suppose that was the whole point of founding the party, as other parties were founded at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina to take part in the elections of 1990. They were elections for the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the Presidency of the republic and there were also elections for the municipal and local assemblies in the -- all the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. We will have a break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, just before we broke, we were talking about the 1990 elections. Can you briefly tell the Court the -- what happened as a result of those elections?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that elections were held at various levels within Bosnia-Herzegovina in November, 1990. The first round of elections were held on the 18th of November, I believe. The results of the elections were very good for the SDS and the other national parties that had been formed in 1990. The SDS gained majorities in the assemblies of -- according to Radovan Karadzic, who was the president of the party, 37 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 37 of the 109 municipalities. On the republic level, the party won, I forget the exact figure, about 75 seats in the two chambers of the republic assembly, and in the elections for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the two candidates of the Serbian nationality who were basically candidates of the SDS were elected to the Presidency, the Presidency was composed of seven people and two of those members had to be of Serbian nationality as well as two of Muslim and Croatian nationality so they elected two members to that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the chamber of -- the two chambers within the assembly. Can you briefly speak about those?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, there were two chambers, the chamber of municipalities so-called and a chamber of citizens. The members of the chamber of municipalities were elected, one from each municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, plus one member from the city of Sarajevo. The city of Sarajevo was a conglomerate of several municipalities each of which elected its own representative to the assembly, for instance, but the city had its own assembly and elected its own separate representative to the chamber of municipalities so there were 110 members in that chamber. The chamber of citizens was based on voting in several constituencies, regional constituencies within the country which united a number of municipalities and each constituency was allotted a certain number of seats, and the distribution of seats was based on the proportional principle, depending on how many people voted for what party in each of those constituencies, then the parties would be assigned a corresponding number of seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Brdjanin the accused in either of the chambers? Was he elected?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, he was elected a deputy in the chamber of municipalities from the municipality of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the results of the elections affect the operations of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the results of the elections had a very interesting impact on the internal operations of the SDS. We spoke earlier about the organisational structure of the party on the basis of its statutes which were basically bodies that were elected by members of the party. The elections resulted in the party having a large number of office holders on various levels and especially important group of office holders were the SDS deputies in the republic assembly who like the other parties that were represented in the assembly weren't what is known as a club of deputies, what we call in the United States, a caucus, that is the group of deputies from that party, who would meet separately and discuss their stands on various issues. So those people got to play a very important role in the governance of Bosnia-Herzegovina obviously, and therefore became very important for the party. The club of deputies met periodically and we in fact have stenographic records of some of those meetings but by no means all of them. What began to happen was that the main board, for instance, which according to the statutes was the body that would meet between the annual assemblies and decide policy didn't really meet that much as the main board and simply the members of the main board, the central leadership of the party, the President Karadzic in particular, began to call meetings at which large numbers of party representatives would be present, including members of the main board, certainly, but also including the deputies and even municipal presidents of the SDS, for instance, sometimes these meetings are called meetings of the deputies clubs, sometimes they are called meetings of the main board, but by and large, the same types of individuals were present at those meetings from the various categories of party and public office holders who were in the SDS, that is the local presidents of the SDS, say, deputies in the assembly, and members of the main board.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P34?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you list at page 151 and following of the main report SDS and other deputies in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, 1991 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, they are listed in an appendix to the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also members of the main board at page 155 and the executive board at page 156?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to what you were saying earlier, that the deputies club being very important, can you take the Chamber to the relevant portion of this exhibit, which is the deputies club meeting minutes of the 28th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly hope so. This is a very lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this meeting, did Karadzic make reference as to who was making the policy within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I'm trying to find the reference. I'm not familiar with this version of the translation. I'm sorry, I'm not having much luck here but there is -- he does say during the course of this meeting, reminding the deputies who were present that they have played a very important role in making policy over the last year, and this was a meeting that was held in February 1992 reminding them that they have made most of the political decisions after discussion in that body rather than the main board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can come back to that, if you wish. The other parts of your reports deal with the government structures. Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the three levels that you outline in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The report and the addendum deal with governmental structures properly speaking in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then in the what became known as the Republika Srpska. The first section of the addendum deals with the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the third section of the main report deals with the -- with Republika Srpska. Those -- and then I believe there is also a subsection in the main report, in part 2, section 2 of the main report that deals with the municipal legal of government in the social Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. Those sections of the reports are based on similar types of documentation to describe the structures of the governing bodies and their operations in so far as information on that was available. They draw on documents such as constitutions and basic legislation which outline the powers, functions and duties of the various organs, and they draw on documents such as the minutes of meetings of those bodies, minutes being short notes of the meetings, more than five pages would be long, but we also have available the stenographic records or even transcripts of audio recordings of many meetings of these bodies. By and large, the -- they -- these sections paint the same picture and as I said the same types of documentation crop up, just different documents, cite in one, where appropriate of course, the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and different section on the Republika Srpska we cite the constitution of Republika Srpska. But they all describe systems which are similar and are typical of the Yugoslav political system, namely the governments at the -- at each level of government and to remind the Court, the levels are starting from the top, the federal level of government, the republic level of government, and basically the municipal level of government, and below that there is a -- what they call a local community, a local level of government which we won't really discuss here but each of those levels of government is based on the principle of having an assembly as the most organ of power on that level. Typically -- not typically but the assembly is defined as the highest organ of power at the given level and the assembly selects an executive organ, variously called the executive committee, executive council, later on in the -- beginning in about 1990, 1991, the government, which carried out the decisions of the assembly and was headed by a president - I don't know if they were called the president of the executive committee or the president of the government. And then on the federal and republic level the assembly would also select a body known as the Presidency, which is a collective body composed of individuals, a different set of individuals, not in the assembly, not in the government, whose basic duty was to represent the given republic or the federation and to carry out other duties, very largely in the area of National Defence, such as developing National Defence plans and that sort of thing, and on the federal level being the Commander-in-Chief in time of war. Typically also the Presidency in times of emergency would be expanded, most particularly in a state of war or imminent threat of war, the Presidency would be expanded to include other office holders such as the president of the executive council, the appropriate military commander on the given level, and other political figures. In addition to that, if the assembly itself were unable to meet because of the nature of the situation, the Presidency, expanded, presumably, would exercise all the authority of the assembly. In other words it - the Presidency - would be able to pass laws and do the other things that the assembly would ordinarily do. That's in an emergency situations. And you find this structure throughout the various levels that are -- that I've mentioned in the federation itself, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that the executive committee would carry out the decisions of the assembly. That body was not independent, was it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: No. The executive committee is the executive body of the assembly, the members are chosen by the assembly and the executive committee reports to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in a time of emergency, the same would apply?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to make a bit of an extrapolation, I think. In an emergency situation, when the assembly is not meeting and the Presidency is exercising the powers of the assembly, then the executive committee would report to the Presidency in so far as the executive committee was able to do anything given the situation. But the president of the executive committee would be a member of the expanded Presidency in those situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've talked about the republic level and also the municipal level. Was there any level in between the two?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really get into the municipal level. I should probably mention that and a couple of other things about the other levels. The peculiarity on the municipal level is that basically it did not have a Presidency that was a separate body, as in the federation and the republic. The chief representative of the municipality was the president of the assembly, and it was only in times of emergency that a so-called Presidency or even a War Presidency would be formed in a municipality, and that would be composed of the same types of office holders as I mentioned before, the president of the assembly, the president of the executive committee, the members of the -- some of the administrative departments of the municipality, including the secretary of National Defence and the head of the police, that sort of thing. And in Republika Srpska I just mention a couple of innovations there in their structure. Typically, the assemblies in the former Yugoslavia were -- had more than one chamber, indeed at certain periods of time they had more than two chambers. In the 1990 elections as I mentioned in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two chambers. The constitution of Republika Srpska provided for an assembly that only had one chamber. Similarly, it did not have a collective Presidency. The constitution of Republika Srpska provided for a president and not a collective body, as a Presidency. I could also mention in that connection with Republika Srpska and its assembly that the original assembly of Republika Srpska, which, I think, is initially called the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was formed in October, 1991, from the deputies club of the Serbian Democratic Party in the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words the SDS deputies club turned itself into the assembly of the Serbian people and later sat as the national assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've now dealt with the two levels. Was there any level in between the two of those?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, you asked about the regional level. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was, in principle, no government -- no level of government in between the republic government and the municipal governments, what they call territorial administrative units. The basic ones were the municipalities. The only exception to that was -- that I mentioned already, alluded to briefly, was the city of Sarajevo which was composed of several municipalities, ten, I believe, who elected from their members a city council, an assembly, if you will, so that the -- Sarajevo had a city government which was based on the municipalities that were part of the city and it elected its own representative to the chamber of municipalities. Aside from that, however, there were -- there was no intermediate level of government between the republic and the municipalities. There was, however, provision in the constitution of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the creation of bodies known as communities of municipalities. These were voluntary associations of municipalities that shared various interests, mostly economic, and they could form an association to promote those interests, economic development, tourism, that type of thing, but they were not -- they did not become territorial administrative units, that is a level of government, per se, that they -- they were strictly a voluntary coordinating type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the area known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina, was there such an association set up?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. In that area, as in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, associations -- there was an association of municipalities which goes back to the 1970s, I believe, the association of municipalities of Banja Luka. However, after the elections of 1990, the SDS became interested in the issue of what are called regionalisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in April, 1991, a new association of municipalities was formed called the association of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, centred in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was appointed president of this association?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, this association had a structure reminiscent of the ones I've been describing. It had an assembly which is composed of the representatives of the municipalities that were members of the association and the assembly elected an executive body similar to a government. Although the association did not have that type of authority but it did elect its own executive body but it did not elect a Presidency so the officers that it elected were a president of the assembly, two vice-presidents of the assembly and then a president of the -- I think they call it the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P67?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is this -- this document is dated the 26th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it refers to the founding session held on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is appointing Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, civil engineer from Celinac, deputy to the chamber of municipalities, to the position of first vice-president; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina passed on the 26th of April, the day that the -- of their founding session, and it elects Mr. Brdjanin as the first vice-president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's signed by --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: It's signed by Vojo Kupresanin as president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an agreement in relation to this community, this association?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The association was set up pursuant to an agreement among the interested municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P69?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is this the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is the agreement on the formation of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take Their Honours very briefly to the important articles within this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Certainly. I would call attention to Article 1 of the agreement which sets out the purpose for the -- its -- the formation of the community of municipalities. It states as being in order to fulfil more rationally and efficiently the common interests and needs of the citizens and coordinate social and economic developments, et cetera. And it names the municipalities that were parties to this agreement. I would then call attention to Article 4, which states that the community would have its own statute, the statute is a document similar to a constitution in the governmental framework or similar to the statute of the Serbian Democratic Party, as Article 4 says, the statute will determine things such as the function of the community municipalities, how they will be performed, the organisation of the organs of the community, et cetera. Now, an interesting feature of this community of municipalities appears in Article 9. I indicated earlier that these communities were formed for the purpose of promoting economic development and that sort of thing. In Article 9, however, we see this new community of municipalities taking responsibility in the area of defence, stating that it will ensure the unity of preparations and the efficiency of the system of all people's defence, take organisational and material and other measures for exercising the rights and duties of citizens in preparations for all people's defence. And that in time of war or imminent threat of war it would organise all people's defence in the territory of the community and also in time of war, it would lead that defence. Those I think are the two most interesting -- or the interesting features of this particular agreement. The copy we have is dated the 29th of April, which is three days after the founding assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your review and analysis of the minutes of the sessions of the -- what's commonly known as the ZOBK, which is the association of municipalities for Bosanska Krajina, was Radoslav Brdjanin an active or inactive participant at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin seems to have been a very active member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P11, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an extract from the minutes of the second session held on the 14th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your statement, could you take the Chamber to the relevant items in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. On page 2 of the translation, at the top, toward the end of agenda item number 2, we see mention of Vice-President Radoslav Brdjanin, who was quoted as proposing that the statute of the community be adopted that day. He says, "I propose to be adopted today as it stands because we cannot have an association of municipalities on a voluntary basis. We cannot wait for public debate in the municipal assemblies and convene the community assembly every month." And after some other speakers intervened, the statute was in fact adopted unanimously according to these minutes. Then in agenda item number 3 a little bit further down that page in the middle at the beginning of the agenda item we see that the Vice-President Brdjanin intervenes again, saying that the chairman and vice-chairman of the executive council should also be elected that day and that the second vice-chairman and members of the executive council could be elected later. And then he goes on to nominate Andjelko Grahovac for the position of chairman of the -- or president of the executive council. And following some debate according to these minutes, that proposal was also adopted, with one vote against. Toward the end of the minutes, under agenda item number 7, we also see Mr. Brdjanin speaking, making a proposal to the assembly that the municipal assemblies in the region cancel their subscription to Radio and Television Sarajevo which had failed to make a broadcast of a statement of the community support for united Yugoslavia. He went on to make some other proposals and these proposals were adopted unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a new document, the statute of the association of municipalities, Bosanska Krajina, and if it can be provisionally marked P2354, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you sure this was not exhibited before?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I've checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You checked, all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, could we just deal very quickly with the articles that you deem important in this statute?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I would just quickly draw attention to again to Article number 1 which lists the municipalities which are to be members of the association. And it says that they have associated themselves in order to realise cooperation and coordination of planning and the realisation of other joint interests. Further articles, for instance, Article 17, Article 17 and 18, deal with -- begin to deal with the organs of the -- of the community, Article 17 and 18 dealing with the assembly, again setting out the structure of the assembly and its responsibilities and then Article 24, which considers the executive organ, stating that the assembly will select an executive council. Article 25 enumerates the -- some of the duties and responsibilities of that council. And then Article 26 sets out the permanent working bodies of the assembly which are similar to the ministries, if you will, of the community namely the political council, economic council, ecological council and a council for National Defence. And then Articles 28 and 29 deal with the officers of the assembly, the president and the vice-presidents. In particular, it notes that the first vice-president deputises for the president of the assembly. And those are the features that we can mention about the statute right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland -- Mr. Treanor, I do notice in Article 26, that there is a specific reference to the peoples defence council as being a permanent working body of the assembly but is there any where else in this statute, any reference to the function of the association as far as defence matters are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is specified in the agreement. Article 27 does say in its enumeration of the duties of the various councils, that the council for National Defence would examine issues in the area of National Defence of interest to the community of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But otherwise you do not have a reflection of the conclusion that was reached to which you referred earlier on from Exhibit P67, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm becoming somewhat concerned because this is now the second document that has been brought to your attention this morning that as far as I know we do not have. We have not been provided. Now, I assume the Prosecutor is going to show me the document that proves they provided it to me but the fact is I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to this statute of the association?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first was the draft statute of the SDS. The second one now is this statute of ZOBK which I can't even find on the list of documents that they said would be used today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The draft statute, if memory serves me correctly, was disclosed yesterday, and the document that we are now looking at, the statute of the ZOBK, was given to you this morning. So you're correct, until this morning, you didn't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I still don't. It wasn't given to me this morning either. Nothing was given to me this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This matter needs to be attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think they've had these for months. I think they've had them for months and to wait until yesterday and this morning to disclose them is just backing ridiculous. We can't possibly -- if they give them to us at 5.00 in one day we can't possibly process them and have them available and useful to us the next morning. I mean that's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent right, Mr. Ackerman. And I think the point is made and taken up by the Trial Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not to be repeated. Fortunately you're not going to start with your cross-examination today so not much harm has been done. But please, Ms. Sutherland, Ms. Korner, try to avoid a repetition of such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I took that into account the fact that Mr. Treanor was not going to be cross-examined today in using the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime I want to make sure that at least Mr. Ackerman can follow what is being stated. Do you have a copy of it now? Please give -- usher, give my copy to Mr. Ackerman and I will -- yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have Exhibit P71 in front of you, which is the third session minutes of the 27th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I don't have the translation yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like someone to check because I remember reading something about this statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the statute of the ZOBK which is very similar in nature which Mr. Treanor will explain later of the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which came into being in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a suspicion, I may be wrong, completely wrong, that this was incorporated in Donja's report. You definitely have used it because I quite remember. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour is right. I recollect taking a witness to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I too recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll do a check. Occasionally these things slip through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not criticising. I'm just making this point because it would also reflect on the objection that was raised by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll tell you what it is. My recollection now is Mr. Ackerman took a witness through it, the statute of the autonomous region and it may have become a Defence Exhibit and that may be why it's not on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour my recollection is this: Dr. Donia spoke of it in his testimony and I think I can even find it here where he did, but I don't think the actual document itself ever came into evidence. Now, there was a time when we used -- but I don't think it's the same document with the witness Ms. Korner is talking about. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. The problem will be resolved anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor you mentioned earlier that Mr. Brdjanin was an active participant at these meetings. What kind of a role did he in fact play?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, he took a very active part in the discussions and introduced some of the more important actions, proposed the initiation of some of the more important actions of the assembly such as electing officers and initiated and conducted discussions on important issues of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just move through a couple of documents briefly, the 27th of May, 1991, which is P71?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This document unlike the previous document or -- is not like the previous document. The previous document represents minutes of a session of the assembly, that is a document that was drawn up after the session, what happened at the session. This is the proposed agenda for the third session of the assembly, which is the only record we have of that particular session, in fact. But from this agenda we can see that the third item, third numbered item on the agenda, is the issue of the status of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was a very important issue of the day indeed, and notes that the rapporteur on this issue would be Radoslav Brdjanin, the vice-president of the assembly of the association.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P72? And then after that, P77?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It can be seen that this is conclusions of a meeting held on the 30th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is actually a resolution passed by the assembly on the 30th of May, 1991. And it deals with the issue of the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia and states among other things, just to summarise briefly for the Court, that any deviation from the constitutional status of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federal republic within federative Yugoslavia would provide the assembly of the community of municipalities with a reason to organise a referendum for the democratic regulation of the constitutional status of Bosnian Krajina as an autonomous or federal region within Yugoslavia. In other words they are taking a position on the future and structure of the Yugoslav state, and item 3 in the conclusions says, specifies that as a deputy to the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and vice-president of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, Radoslav Brdjanin is assigned to inform republican assembly of these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P77?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 1st of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This document is a decision which was taken at a joint session of the SDS regional board, and the association of municipalities on the 31st of July, 1991, and the decision basically recommends Nedjeljko Kesic for a position within the security services centre in Banja Luka and it is signed by Radoslav Brdjanin for the community of municipalities and it says for the personnel commission. I'm not sure what personnel commission that is, whether it's of the regional SDS board or of the association of municipalities and it's also signed by Radislav Vukic for the regional board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so this document -- is this document showing that the parties are having -- are proposing a candidate for within the police structure?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, as I say the decision basically recommends Nedjeljko Kesic for the position of chief of the state security service sector in the Banja Luka security services centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned briefly in your testimony earlier, the interparty agreements between the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a new document? And this is an intercept dated the 17th of August, 1991, provisionally marked as P2355.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a -- the conversation -- an intercept of a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Nenad Stevandic. Are you aware of who the person Nenad Stevandic is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Nenad Stevandic, as far as I know, is a local SDS politician in -- from Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take the Court to the relevant part of this intercept in relation to the accused, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, there are a couple of interesting parts in this conversation. For instance, at the bottom of page 1, Radovan Karadzic asks Mr. Stevandic what it's like as concerns the political situation, and they go on to -- Mr. Stevandic goes on to say that, well, Andjelko, Andjelko Grahovac is the chairman of the executive committee of the community and Vojo Kupresanin, the president of the assembly, are going forward, full tilt, quite recklessly. Brdjanin would like to put a stop to it to have a bit of consultation and reasoning. And Karadzic goes on to say, to tell them not to do anything stupid, seeming to agree with him that Grahovac and Kupresanin might be going too far. A little bit further on, at the top of page 1, Karadzic remarks, "Yes, we will do everything that Vojo and Brdjo think but after the failure of the agreements that Alija will bring about, we will accuse Alija for the failure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, it's page 2, not page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the top of page 2, continuing on the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are at page 2, sir, I would like you to explain what you understand by the next bit of conversation, "And I have a hold of Brdjanin, last time we took him fishing up to Jovica." What do you understand by that? Who is Jovica, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure who Jovica is. Presumably another local politician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It couldn't be Jovica Stanisic by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And do you understand anything by "we took him fishing up to Jovica"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you take it literally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I take that literally. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You take that literally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went on a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Further on in this conversation, there is a -- perhaps another interesting passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that on page 5 of the English translation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is, I'm trying to compare it with the original. Stevandic tells Karadzic, "One thing is enough" - this is in the middle, the top third of page 5 - "One thing is enough we went to Jovica's and three names have remained that could become official, I, Miroslav and Brdjanin." Karadzic says, "Yup." And Stevandic says, "Since we put Brdjanin into the picture he's not letting Vojo and Andjelko do anything stupid. However, all of them have now turned against Brdjanin, Zoran, Andjelko and Vojo, not because of jealousy but because they wanted to become involved in this part of the work for reasons that I don't even know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For some reason the translation I have and the one that Mr. Treanor has are fairly dramatically different. Mine says that these say completely different things than what Mr. Treanor's translation says. I don't have any explanation about that at all but I do have a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does your translation say, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mine says, with that paragraph that he just read, for instance, "Now that we've included Brdjanin into the scheme, he won't allow Vojo, he said let them be stupid but Zoran and Andjelko and Vojo they all turned against Brdjanin not out of jealousy but because they wanted to be involved in that part of the job and someone should ..." It's consists, you know, fairly different language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read yours? I don't know. What I have is pretty much similar to what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour we had these documents were initially translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then revised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. What is the ERN number on your page, Mr. Ackerman? Is it 03075743?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No it's 01048636 Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it. So what I have and what probably the witness -- expert witness has is an updated translation, which I suggest can and should be made available to Mr. Ackerman, because obviously he's got a previous --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was disclosed to Mr. Ackerman, this new translation, last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I see Mr. Ackerman looking at the lap top or the notebook that he has, so... Anyway this can be sorted out, Mr. Ackerman, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so you'll all know what's happening, almost every day we get a new stack of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know but you're not the only one, Mr. Ackerman, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not possible for us to keep up and if they gave them to us Friday that explains it because we just have not been able to get all that material processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've got two volunteers working almost full time and we still can't keep up. These are all materials that they've had for months and months and months and I just don't know why we are getting them all of a sudden right now. It just is not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we are finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. It's for Ms. Sutherland to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have finished with that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P16, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the number given to this document? Because I missed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a -- dated the 6th of September, 1991 and it is a -- entitled a public statement. And it refers to a meeting held on the 6th of September, 1991. Can you tell the -- Their Honours the importance of this document, which leads into the next?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, this is an interesting document. I mentioned earlier the main organs of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, namely the assembly and the executive council, and I believe I mentioned the fact that similar to the municipalities but unlike the republic and the federation, that assembly did not have a Presidency, that is it did not elect a separate group of individuals to a body of that name which was specified as such in the statute. This document however does make reference to a Presidency and indeed to a session of that Presidency of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina which was held on the 6th of September, 1991. I would have to conclude, since the -- such a Presidency is not mentioned in the statute, that the term here is being used to describe a meeting of the president of the assembly and the first vice-president and the second vice-president. That is they are meeting as a separate body and issuing a statement on an important issue of the day, namely the fighting that's going on in Croatia, and they -- in the name of the assembly of the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities, they demand an immediate end to the shooting and killing of Serbian people in Okucani and Stara Gradiska, which are towns in Croatia just across the river from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a new document? It's an undated document, disclosure number 4.223. If that can be provisionally marked P2356? Your Honours, the ERN number of the translation is 0110-2452. And if we can put the document on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor this document is undated but the -- is the content of the document the same as the document we just looked at, P16, dated the 6th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, the document refers to similar subject matter from which I would conclude that it was, although undated, issued about the same time as the previous document. It refers to the situation in Okucani and Stara Gradiska. And goes on interestingly at the end of the paragraph number 2, "This does not mean that we are preparing ourselves for war but it is our holy duty to defend the Serbian people first and foremost and by doing so, Yugoslavia as well." And at the top of the document, we can see that this is a statement issued by Radoslav Brdjanin, vice-president of the assembly of the association of Bosnian Krajina, making a statement I would translate that on the question of defence, the translation I have says department of defence. But I believe that we have him here making a statement on the issue of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P12? This is an extract from the minutes of the 7th session of the ZOBK, held on the 16th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this -- what was dealt with at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, this meeting was a very important occasion in the developments of the Bosnian Krajina. At this meeting, the association of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina changed itself into what it called the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The document is an extract from the records of that meeting. The first item on the agenda is a consideration of a decision on proclaiming an Autonomous Region of Krajina and further down the page, under number 1, we see that the vice-president -- vice-president of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, Radoslav Brdjanin, made a statement in that connection which reads, "By this decision we are ensuring the region's independence. We do not want to bother anyone who does not want to leave Yugoslavia but nobody here can be allowed to put various kinds of pressure on us. Failure to construct major facilities, oil shortage," et cetera. "The BH Presidency again refused today to go to Belgrade to negotiate. We are for peace but we do not want that peace to be implemented over our faces, as Tudjman and the other leaders want. We all know that the Serbs support the army, by declaring autonomy we want to go to negotiations, not to war." And then this extract from the record indicates that they held a vote and the deputies voted unanimously to declare the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn now to Exhibit P81, which is dated -- which is a decision on the proclamation of the SAO Krajina, and it's dated the 16th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision that the assembly passed pursuant to the remarks made by Mr. Brdjanin. I would point out two features of this decision. One is contained in Article 1, which states that the -- what the translation here calls the "alliance" but it's "The community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina declared the Autonomous Region of Krajina as an autonomous democratic unit of sovereign citizens and peoples and an inseparable part of federative Yugoslavia as a federal state which consists of the republics of Serbia and Montenegro and other federal units which have expressed their free will to remain in this federal state." This is the language which is not contained in these founding documents of the original community of municipalities. This is -- this article, in fact, indicates that the autonomous region is being established in order to be and remain a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia.
